newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Court told Macquarie's Hannes is also Booth.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Court told Macquarie's Hannes is also Booth.

text.p: An executive director of Macquarie Bank Ltd Simon Hannes was named in a New South Wales court on Monday as being the fictious TNT Ltd options trader Mark Booth.
Hannes' lawyer Ian Barker, QC, told the court that his client would plead not guilty to the charges laid under the Financial Transactions Act relating to non-reporting of large cash transactions.

"It is also alleged that the defendant on September 9, using the name Mark Booth or M. Booth, conducted the following non-reportable transactions amounting to A$81,900," the office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) said in a statement of facts lodged with the court.
The statement detailed a series of cash withdrawals from a Commonwealth Bank of Australia bank account held by Hannes on September 9 last year from various branches around Sydney.
The amounts were for A$9,900 or less. A financial transaction must be reported under the Financial Transactions Reports Act if above A$10,000.
The DPP statement said Hannes then went to a series of bank branches around Sydney and used the cash withdrawn from his account to obtain nine bank cheques totalling A$81,900.

"On September 10, 1996, the nine bank cheques obtained by the defendant were paid into an Ord Minnett Cash Management Trust Account in the name of M. Booth. These funds were subsequently used to acquire a substantial quantity of call options in TNT Ltd securities shortly prior to the announcement of the takeover of TNT Ltd," the DPP said.
Hannes said in an interview with the DPP on January 17 that he withdrew the cash on September 6 and September 9.
Hannes said these funds were withdrawn "to give to an unnamed person with whom he had formed an investment syndicate", the DPP said.
"The defendant claimed that he had been advised by bank officers that the amount of cash that he wanted could not be obtained from one branch," it said.
"He further claimed that the unnamed person subsequently requested that he obtain cheques so that they could be paid to an Ord Minnett Cash Management Account.
"The defendant stated that he then used the cash he had previously withdrawn to obtain bank cheques."
Macquarie Bank said late last month that Hannes had been charged and that he intended to plead not guilty.
The investment bank was the adviser to TNT Ltd on the eventually successful takeover bid for the transport group by Dutch telecommunications and postal group Koninklijke PTT Nederland NV (KPN).
Hannes is a senior executive of the bank's corporate advisory division, but was not part of the team working on the TNT transaction, Macquarie said then.
KPN annnounced an agreed A$2.0 billion bid for TNT on October 2 which completely surprised the market.
Mark Booth made about A$2.0 million in profits from trading in TNT options which had been virtually worthless before KPN's A$2.45 per share cash offer for TNT.
TNT's shares had been trading around A$1.60 at the time. Booth spent about A$90,000 on the options transactions.

Mark Buscombe, a lawyer for the DPP, told the court that Hannes was fully aware of of the A$10,000 limit for reporting transactions and that "the transactions of the 9th were clearly designed to avoid reporting requirements."
"The prosecution case is a strong one," Buscombe said.
Hannes was ordered at the hearing to report to police every Monday as part of his bail conditions, under which he has also handed over his passport.
A prosecution request to make Hannes report to police three times a week was denied.
The next court hearing date was set for March 3. Hannes has yet to formally enter a plea.
